title: Genesis 10:21–32
context: The table turns to Shem, father of Eber, then Peleg and Joktan, and closes: from these clans the nations spread abroad after the flood.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Shem, Eber, and the spreading of the clans after the flood: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The description of Shem, Ge 10:21, we have not only his name, Shem, which signifies a name; but two titles to distinguish him by. He was the father of all the children of Eber. Eber was his great grandson, but why should he be called the father of all his children, rather than of all Arphaxad's or Salah's?
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 10:21)

reformed.quote: Moses, being about to speak of the sons of Shem, makes a brief introduction, which he had not done in reference to the others. Nor was it without reason; for since this was the race chosen by God, he wished to sever it from other nations by some special mark. This also is the reason why he expressly styles him the father of the sons of Eber,' and the elder brother of Japheth.

verses.text: Children were also born to Shem (the elder brother of Japheth), the father of all the children of Eber.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shem is introduced with honor: father of all the children of Eber, and Japheth’s elder brother. The line that will include Abraham is a family among families, not a denial of the others already listed.

Arminian readers gladly trace the Messiah’s ancestors here, while insisting God’s mercy remains wide: Shem’s privilege serves the blessing of the nations, not a closed circle of grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Father of all the children of Eber” flags the line of promise. Eber yields the family from which Abraham comes; Shem is placed to carry the story toward Christ.

God sovereignly marks this branch. Among all the Table’s names, providence highlights Shem and Eber because the election of a people for the world’s good is already in view.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor Shem and Eber. Arminians typically read this line as the appointed means of a sincere, wide blessing for the nations; Reformed interpreters usually read it as God’s sovereign choice of the promise-bearing family that will run to Abraham and Christ.

verses.text: The sons of Shem were: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shem’s sons include Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram—eastern and northern peoples as well as the ancestor of the Hebrews’ nearer kin.

Even the promise line sits among brothers. Asshur and Aram will later be empires and neighbors; they remain kin in this list. God’s blessing of Shem is larger than one grandson.
verses.reformedNotes:
Five sons, one of whom (Arpachshad) will carry the recorded line to Eber and Abraham. God names the others because they too are ordered under His rule.

The promise narrows without pretending the other sons do not exist. Sovereignty can distinguish a line while still governing Elam and Asshur.

verses.text: The sons of Aram were: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.
verses.arminianNotes:
Aram’s sons include Uz—later associated with Job’s land. Wisdom and suffering will arise from this branch too.

Arminians hear that God attends to Aramean families with the same naming care. Cultures north and east of Canaan are gift, not narrative leftovers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Aram’s grandsons are catalogued because the Lord numbers Israel’s neighbors in advance.

Uz and his brothers exist by providence. The God of the Table is already the God of the east.

verses.text: Arpachshad became the father of Shelah. Shelah became the father of Eber.
verses.arminianNotes:
The chain tightens: Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber. Ordinary fathering is how God keeps a line in the world.

Classical Arminians see responsible history in begetting and naming—human families as the means of blessing—while tracing with the church the road that will reach Abraham.
verses.reformedNotes:
Three links, no gaps: God is preserving the spine of the genealogy that will later extend to Abraham and, in the fullness of time, to Christ.

Providence over genealogies is meticulous. The line toward Abraham is not a lucky survival of names; it is God’s keeping.

verses.text: To Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided. His brother’s name was Joktan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Peleg is named for a division of the earth in his days—often linked to the scattering of Babel in the next chapter, or to a splitting of territories. Joktan is named beside him without that etymology.

Classical Arminians read the division as a historical event under providence that still involves human pride (the tower) and human spreading. The earth is divided “in his days,” a responsible moment in the nations’ story, not a denial of God’s care for every resulting people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator pauses to interpret a name: Peleg because the earth was divided. God timestamps a global ordering of peoples.

Division of the earth is by God’s act, not demographic accident. In Peleg’s days the Lord apportioned the world—setting the stage on which He will call Abraham from among the nations.
verses.keyContrast: Both tie Peleg’s name to a division of the earth. Arminians highlight a historical spreading (often linked to Babel’s pride) in which human responsibility and God’s wide care for resulting nations meet; Reformed interpreters typically emphasize God’s sovereign dividing of peoples and lands as decree, preparing the line of Eber toward Abraham.

verses.text: Joktan became the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
verses.arminianNotes:
Joktan’s many sons begin here—names associated with southern and eastern clans. The brother not named for division still fathers a full household.

Blessing is not only on Peleg’s side. Joktan’s children display the gift of fruitfulness among Shem’s other branches.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list of Joktanites is long because God records more than the promise spine. He is Lord of the many as well as of the few.

Providence over genealogies includes the populous side of Eber. These names are in Scripture because the Lord willed their memory.

verses.arminianNotes:
Three more sons, briefly named. The Table refuses to rush past them.

Arminians hear dignity in the briefest list: God knows Hadoram, Uzal, and Diklah. Wideness of mercy begins with being named before Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The genealogy continues without ornamental comment. God is counting.

Stories unknown to us still sit inside named decree. These sons exist because the Lord ordered Eber’s house.

verses.arminianNotes:
Sheba appears again (compare Ham’s line)—trade names can overlap in the ancient record, or related peoples can share a name. Either way, southern wealth is on the map.

God is not confused by overlapping names. Cultures of incense and gold are still families first, gifts under providence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Obal, Abimael, and Sheba take their place in Joktan’s roster. The Lord of nations is precise even when later readers must sort shared names.

Overlapping names do not threaten providence. God knows which Sheba He means in each text.

verses.text: Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ophir and Havilah close the list with lands later famed for gold. “All these were the sons of Joktan” gathers a large family as one household.

Arminians give thanks for material gifts and for many sons: prosperity and people are from God’s hand, to be received without pride.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary line is bookkeeping under God: all these belong to Joktan in His record.

Gold-lands and ordinary names alike exist by the Lord’s appointment. The Table’s “all these” is a completeness claim—God has not missed a son He meant to list.

verses.text: Their dwelling extended from Mesha, as you go toward Sephar, the mountain of the east.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joktan’s sons receive a territory description, as Canaan’s sons did. Eastward hills and named bounds mean these clans had a home.

Application: land is gift. God gives peoples room to live; cultures take shape in geography under a providence that is kind, not stingy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Borders for Joktan match the pattern used for Canaan: God assigns space as well as ancestry.

Territories exist by decree. Mesha toward Sephar is not a random range; the Lord set the eastern hill country as their dwelling.

verses.text: These are the sons of Shem, by their families, according to their languages, lands, and nations.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shem’s section closes with the same fourfold refrain as Japheth’s coastlands and Ham’s sons. Shem is one nation-family among the three, even as his line carries special promise.

Arminians hold both: gratitude for the Eber–Abraham road, and refusal to treat other Shemite nations as extras. Languages and lands among Shem’s children are gifts of a God whose mercy is sincerely wide.
verses.reformedNotes:
The refrain again: clans, languages, lands, nations. Shem’s diversity is structured by God.

The promise line does not dissolve the Table into one clan. God ordered many Shemite nations while keeping Eber’s thread for Abraham and Christ.

verses.text: These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their generations, according to their nations. The nations divided from these on the earth after the flood.
verses.arminianNotes:
The chapter’s seal: clans, genealogies, nations, then spreading abroad after the flood. From one family, a world of peoples—exactly the filling of the earth God intended.

Classical Arminians read this as blessing: God wants the nations, not a single empire. Spreading is gift and calling; the next chapter will show pride trying to halt it. Mercy remains wide to every people that came from these sons.
verses.reformedNotes:
The closing sentence is decree-shaped: from these, nations spread. The Table is not anthropology alone; it is theology of providence.

The post-flood world of peoples exists because God willed it. Genealogies, nations, and their spreading prepare the stage for Abraham—and, in the fullness of time, for the Christ who gathers the nations without erasing what God has made.
verses.keyContrast: Both see the nations’ spread after the flood as God’s purpose, not accident. Arminians emphasize blessing, responsible history, and sincere wideness of mercy toward every people from Noah; Reformed commentators emphasize sovereign ordering of genealogies and territories, the earth filled by decree, and the Table as the set stage for Abraham and Christ.
